title: Nyaya (logic)
hook: a bell is struck and fades, and a Nyaya teacher turns that fading into an argument in five steps

segments.voice: This week began with the long night of Maha Shivaratri and turned to a new part of the path: the six darshanas, schools of thought, set side by side and never ranked. Yesterday was Nyaya, the school of logic. Where did you catch yourself jumping to a conclusion? Today closes the week. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-two.
screen: `FROM SHIVA'S NIGHT TO THE SIX SCHOOLS.` · `NYAYA, CONTINUED.`

segments.voice: Somebody strikes a bell. The note blooms out into the room, hangs there, thins, and then it's gone. Nobody in the room is surprised. Of course it faded. But a teacher of Nyaya would stop you right there and ask: how do you know it had to fade? You heard this one bell. You didn't hear every sound there will ever be. So what gave you the right to say that sound doesn't last? Nyaya takes that small, ordinary leap and slows it down until you can see every step. Today the school shows one of its tools: an argument built in five parts, said out loud, so the other person can check each one.
screen: `A BELL, AND THEN SILENCE.` → `HOW DO YOU KNOW IT HAD TO FADE?` → `AN ARGUMENT IN FIVE PARTS.`

segments.voice: The Nyaya Sutra names the five parts of an argument: the proposition, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion. Its early commentator, Vatsyayana, walks them through with sound itself, and it goes something like this. One: sound does not last. Two: because it is produced. Three: whatever is produced does not last, like a clay pot. Four: sound, too, is produced. Five: so sound does not last. At first it sounds slow, even a little silly. You said the same thing twice. But look at step three, because that's where the whole thing lives. It names the rule out loud, and then it points to a case both people have seen with their own eyes. Pots get made, and pots break. An argument in Nyaya is not one mind talking to itself. It's two people looking at the same pot. If you can't point to a shared case where your rule plainly holds, the argument doesn't stand. And because the rule is said out loud, the other person can test it. Not everyone agreed with this one, by the way. Thinkers of the Mimamsa school held that the sounds of the Veda are eternal, and they argued the point with Nyaya. Nyaya's answer was not to shout louder. It was to lay out the steps, so the disagreement could land on the step where it really lived. Now bring it home. A friend doesn't text back. One: they're upset with me. Two: because they haven't answered. Three: whoever doesn't answer is upset, like… and there you stop. Where's your pot?
screen: `FIVE PARTS, SAID OUT LOUD.` · `SOUND DOESN'T LAST, LIKE A POT.` · `THE EXAMPLE DOES THE REAL WORK.` · `NAME THE STEP YOU DISAGREE WITH.` · then, large: `WHERE'S YOUR POT?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to a sound fade, then test one conclusion. Settle, and let the breath slow. If there's a bell or a chime nearby, strike it once; if not, just listen to whatever sound comes next, and follow it all the way down into quiet. Then bring to mind one rule of thumb you live by, something like: anyone who's late doesn't care, or whatever's cheap breaks. Say the rule to yourself. Then look for the pot: a real case, one you've actually seen, where that rule plainly held. Then look for a case where it didn't. If the pot is there, good. If it isn't, let the rule loosen its grip. If you pray, you can rest in the name of God you use as the silence settles. The bell holds the time.
Nyaya. The school of logic, and its argument in five parts: a claim, a reason, an example you can both see, the fit, and the conclusion.
Your line: Nyaya, logic. Today, when you hear yourself give a reason, find your pot: one real case where your rule held. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: In traditional Sanskrit schools, students meet Nyaya through the Nyaya Sutra and its commentaries, learning to set out an argument step by step and to test it in discussion with a teacher.

original.note: Sanskrit: nyaya, the name of the school of logic and reasoning.

trapdoor: what you thought: logic is a dry thing for classrooms.
what it means: in Nyaya, a good argument is said out loud in five parts, so someone else can check every step.
what a scholar hears: the Nyaya Sutra lists the five members of an argument; Vatsyayana's commentary illustrates them with sound, which is produced, like a pot.

notes: Editor pass: cut the superlative 'most famous tool' and 'at length'; Vatsyayana's example now 'sound itself'; replaced the stock 'ordinary Tuesday' line; practice and carry changed from a conclusion about someone (which 1161 just used) to testing a rule of thumb you live by.
Week end (days 1156–1162). The review names Shivaratri and the start of the darshanas without detail, since 1160–1161 were written by another writer; check it fits what they taught.

The five members (pratijna, hetu, udaharana, upanaya, nigamana) per Nyaya Sutra 1.1.32; the sound/pot illustration is attributed to Vatsyayana's Bhashya. Confirm that Vatsyayana's example is sound and a pot or dish (sthali), and that 'early commentator' is fair.
The smoke-and-fire example was deliberately avoided in case 1160–1161 used it.
Mimamsa's view that Vedic sound/word is eternal, and its debate with Nyaya, is stated without ranking; confirm the phrasing is fair to Mimamsa.
